## Assignment

### Interpretation (required)

In 2–4 sentences, state in plain language what your result means in the context of the problem, and identify one assumption or limitation of this analysis and why it matters.


Create plots for normal, t, and F distributions using ggplot's `stat_function()` layer. 

Provide a brief description of each distribution and an example of how it is used. Include descriptive titles, sub-titles, axis labels

### Normal distribution

From the `dnorm` help page:

>dnorm gives the density . . . of the normal distribution.

The y-axis is the "probability density"

From NIST e-Handbook

>For a continuous function, the probability density function (pdf) is the probability that the variate has the value x. Since for continuous distributions the probability at a single point is zero, this is often expressed in terms of an integral between two points.

```{r}
tibble(x = c(-3, 3)) |> 
  ggplot() +
  stat_function(aes(x), fun = dnorm) +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Distrubtion using `dnorm()` function",
    subtitle = "Baseline for many statisitical checks which assume data follows a 'normal' distribution",
    y = "Probability Density"
  )
```

#### Critical values for 95% probabilities for two-tailed distribution

```{r}
qnorm(1 - 0.05/2)
qnorm(0.05/2)
```



Probability of finding a value between -1.9 and +1.96 is ~95%

```{r}
pnorm(1.96) - pnorm(-1.96)
```



For each distribution, provide the critical value(s) used to estimate 95% probability. (Only one example is needed if multiple distributions are possible.) Describe if you are using a "one-tailed" or "two-tailed" value.

### t-distribution

```{r}
tibble(x = c(-3, 3)) |> 
  ggplot() +
  stat_function(aes(x), fun = dt, args = list(df = 4), color = "blue") +
  stat_function(aes(x), fun = dt, args = list(df = 30), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  stat_function(aes(x), fun = dnorm) +
  labs(
    title = "Student t Distrubtion using `dt()` function",
    subtitle = "Used when sampling is limited; approaches normal distribution when number of samples is >30",
    y = "Probability Density"
  )
```

#### Critical values for df = 9 for two-taild distribution

```{r}
qt(0.05/2, df = 9, lower.tail = FALSE)
qt(0.05/2, df = 9)
```

Probability of finding a value between -2.26 and 2.26 for a t-distribution with df = 9

```{r}
pt(2.26, df = 9) - pt(-2.26, df = 9)
```



### F-distribution

```{r}
tibble(x = c(0, 5)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x)) +
  stat_function(fun = df, args = list(df1 = 2, df2 = 2), color = "blue") +
  stat_function(fun = df, args = list(df1 = 9, df2 = 2), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  stat_function(fun = df, args = list(df1 = 29, df2 = 29), color = "black") +
  stat_function(fun = df, args = list(df1 = 99, df2 = 99), color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "F distrubtion using `df()` function",
    subtitle = "Commonly used to create control limits for standard deviation control charts.\nDepends on sampling of two processes",
    y = "Probability Density"
  )
```

#### Critical value for F-distribution for df1 = 9 and df2 = 2 (single-tail distribution)

```{r}
qf(0.95, df1 = 9, df2 = 2)
```
